content: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a prevalent and often painful condition in children. It can sometimes lead to tympanic membrane perforation and, in some cases, progress to chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM). The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of long-term antibiotic use (lasting six weeks or more) in preventing AOM, AOM with tympanic membrane perforation, and CSOM. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, OLD MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to August 2010. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials comparing long-term antibiotics with either placebo or no treatment in the prevention of AOM, AOM with perforation, or CSOM. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors. The outcomes assessed included the occurrence of AOM, the number of AOM episodes, recurrent AOM, overall episodes of illness, side effects, antibiotic resistance, and outcomes both during and after the intervention. For dichotomous outcomes, summary risk ratios (RR) were calculated using fixed and random-effects models. For rate-based outcomes, summary incidence rate ratios (IRR) were determined. Seventeen studies involving a total of 1,586 children were included in the analysis. All studies focused on children at increased risk of AOM, with seven studies specifically targeting children prone to otitis media. Most of the studies were of high quality, and 16 of them provided data relevant to the primary outcomes. Only one study reported on AOM with perforation or CSOM. The findings demonstrated that long-term antibiotic use significantly reduced the likelihood of experiencing any episode of AOM (14 studies, 1,461 children; RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.79, random-effects model). Additionally, the number of AOM episodes was significantly reduced (13 studies, 1,327 children; IRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.66, random-effects model). On average, treating five children with long-term antibiotics would prevent one child from experiencing AOM during the treatment period. Furthermore, for every 12 months of treatment, antibiotics prevented approximately 1.5 episodes of AOM per child. The analysis also explored statistical heterogeneity. Importantly, long-term antibiotic use was not associated with a significant increase in adverse events (12 studies, 817 children; RR 1.99, 95% CI 0.25 to 15.89, random-effects model). In conclusion, for children at increased risk of AOM, administering antibiotics once or twice daily reduces the likelihood of AOM while the child is on treatment. In similar populations, the number of AOM episodes per year can be reduced from approximately three to 1.5. The absolute benefits of this intervention are likely to be greater in high-risk children. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these conclusions.
